title: Exposing the fabrications
hookLine: fabricated reports spread, and scholars worked hard to expose them

cards: A man stands in a gathering and says he heard a certain shaykh, in a certain city. He names the shaykh, the street, the season. Very convincing.
A scholar in the room asks one quiet question: in what year did you hear him? The man answers. And the scholar says: that shaykh had already died by then.

The report collapses. Scenes like this are told about the hadith scholars, and the early scholar Sufyan al-Thawri is reported to have put it simply: when the narrators used lies, we used history against them.

teach.b: First, the warning. Three days ago we met the report carried by so many chains: whoever lies about the Prophet ﷺ on purpose, let him take his seat in the Fire.
The introduction to Sahih Muslim has a quieter one, aimed not at the forger but at the forwarder: it is enough of a lie for a person to pass on everything he hears. So the duty runs two ways.
Don't invent, and don't simply repeat.
Why people forged: the scholars were frank about it. Some wanted to win an argument between factions. Some were storytellers after a bigger crowd.
Some wanted favor from a ruler. And some, as the scholars tell it, meant well.
They report a man who admitted inventing reports about the reward for reciting each surah of the Qur'an, because he thought people were drifting from it. Good intentions didn't save the report.
A lie about the Prophet stayed a lie.
How they caught them: every tool from this block came out. The chain: did these people meet? The narrators: who was he, and how was his memory?
The dates: was the shaykh even alive? The text: does it promise a mountain for a pebble, or clash with the Qur'an? And they wrote it down.
Scholars compiled whole books of fabricated reports, such as Ibn al-Jawzi's collection of forgeries, so a false saying could be named and recognized, not quietly forgotten and later revived.
A forged hadith in a book of forgeries is a lie with a warning label tied around its neck.

how: Hadith scholars identify fabricated reports by examining chains, narrators, dates and texts, and compiled books of forgeries; Muslim teachers today often caution against sharing sayings attributed to the Prophet without a source and a grade.

o: the scholars' habit of hiding which reports were false

games.q: a man says he heard a shaykh in a certain year. you know when that shaykh died. what's your next move?
o: take his word; he named the street.
ask him the year, and check it against the shaykh's death.
add the report to your book anyway.
games.why: the scholars asked the year. if the shaykh was already dead, the story collapsed: history used against lies.

practice: Recall the last message that began with something like "the Prophet said", "scientists say" or "a well-known person once said".
Run it through the scholars' tools: who sent it and where did they get it, is there a source, does it promise too much, does a date not fit? If you can't answer, you have your answer: not yet.

wordCard.voice: Exposing the fabrications. The scholars' work of catching forged reports, by chain, by narrator, by date and by text, and naming them in books so they couldn't hide. Today's word.

orig.note: fabricated: the name for a forged report.

carryVoice: Your line: they checked. Good intentions never saved a forged report. See you next time.
